paras: The lynching of Amos Randall, Dan Kennedy and Henry Golden was the killing by a mob of one white man and two Black men at Mulberry, Polk County, Florida, early on May 20, 1903. Accused of murdering Barney Brown, a white prohibition worker, they were shot by armed men described as unmasked and prominent in the county, and a coroner's jury blamed "persons unknown." Editors remarked chiefly on a white man being lynched with two Black men.

Polk County voted on liquor in a "wet or dry" election that closed May 19, and Brown, a Mulberry resident of about 60, had worked for the dry side. Randall, a white man from Pennsylvania, was said to keep a "blind tiger," an illegal liquor shop; earlier in May a Black watchman guarding his premises found dynamite on his porch. On the night of May 18 Brown was shot from ambush on the road home from Bartow and his throat was cut, and an inquest adjourned without a clue.

Accounts of the seizure differ. An Associated Press dispatch from Bartow said Kennedy and Golden, guards at Randall's premises, were questioned before Justice Cain's court and then taken "out into the darkness" by an armed crowd, where Golden said Randall had followed Brown and shot him. A Tampa dispatch said instead that all three were in custody, that one Black man confessed Randall had hired them, and that the trio were taken out about 3 a.m. and lynched.

The New York Sun's Tampa account was the most detailed: Golden was dragged into the town square and shot, and Kennedy, who refused to talk, was tied to a tree and hit by more than 150 bullets. The mob then fired into Randall's house, shot him down as he ran with his rifle, and riddled his body under a church. Joe Jacobs, a whiskey salesman staying with Randall, told the Daytona Gazette-News that volleys struck the house at daybreak, that Randall went out saying "I'll die game if they come for me again," and that he himself fled without seeing the killing. According to the Sun, the bodies were shown in the public square to crowds from across the county.

Sheriff Tillis arrived from Bartow about two hours later, and a coroner's jury found the three killed "at the hands of persons unknown." The bodies were buried at noon, officers seized about half a carload of whiskey at Randall's place, and the AP reported that no arrests were likely; no later arrest or trial appears in the coverage. The Sun added that nearly every Black resident near Mulberry left, idling the phosphate mines.

The wire stories ran on May 20 and 21 from Georgia to Maine and Arizona, under headlines such as "Mob Avenges Murder by Triple Killing," with the Black men's names spelled half a dozen ways. Southern editors read the killings as a blow against illegal liquor: the Hattiesburg Daily Progress called it "illegal, though effective," and the Gainesville Star, while regretting it, said it showed public sentiment against blind tigers. The Florida Times-Union was "sorry those three murderers were lynched," and the Madison New Enterprise held such affairs "to be deplored by all citizens."

The Black press carried the wire story with no reporting of its own; the Savannah Tribune printed the syndicated text that also ran in the Gainesville Star. The St. Paul Appeal added, "This is a case of social equality that was not very desirable," and the Colored American found most noteworthy that a white man "said to have instigated the deed" was lynched too. The Seattle Republican and the Chicago Broad Ax listed all three among the year's lynchings, while the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate retold the case as "Another Martyr to Temperance."

Reports disagree on the hour (2 a.m., 3 a.m. or daybreak), the mob's size (twenty-five, fifty or a hundred) and whether it was masked. Most said the men were shot, but the Gainesville Star wrote that all three were hanged on one tree, and the Spokane Press alone said the questioned men had been "allowed to go" before the raid.

accounts.label: AP dispatch from Bartow
accounts.gist: Kennedy and Golding were questioned before Justice Cain's court, taken into the darkness by an armed crowd, and Golding said Randall shot Brown; about 25 men fired some 200 shots at Randall's bar; Randall returned fire.

accounts.label: Tampa wire
accounts.gist: All three were in custody, one Black man confessed Randall hired them, and the trio were taken out about 3 a.m. (2 a.m. in one version) and lynched by about fifty unmasked prominent men.

accounts.label: New York Sun's Tampa correspondent
accounts.gist: Golden confessed and was shot in the town square; Kennedy was tied to a tree and shot; Randall was shot fleeing his house; mob of 100 including officials; inquest found 'persons unknown'.

accounts.label: Gainesville Star (Florida)
accounts.gist: 'Aleck Kennedy' and Golden confessed after arrest; all three were lynched on the same tree and left hanging.

accounts.label: Joe Jacobs, Randall's guest (Daytona Gazette-News)
accounts.gist: The mob fired volleys into the house at daybreak; Randall went out with his gun; Jacobs fled and did not see the killing; he says the Tampa Tribune's account of him was wrong.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire under headlines like 'Three Lynched Near Tampa' and 'Mob Avenges Murder by Triple Killing', presenting the confession as fact.
Hattiesburg Daily Progress: 'new way of breaking up blind tigers', 'illegal, though effective'; 'That closed the blind tiger shop.'
Florida Times-Union 'sorry those three murderers were lynched'; Gainesville Star calls it regrettable but possibly for good; Deland News says lynching all tiger men 'will not do'.
Madison New Enterprise: 'to be deplored by all citizens'; the community suffers in outside eyes.
Savannah Tribune ran the syndicated text without comment, headlined as an 'alleged' murder.
St. Paul Appeal's ironic 'social equality' line and the Colored American's note that a white man was lynched too; Seattle Republican lists it under 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign'.
Wisconsin Weekly Advocate, a temperance column, mourns Brown as 'Another Martyr to Temperance' and reports the lynching without criticism.
